h1: How nitrogen gas gives nitro stouts their creamy head
title: How nitro stouts get a creamy head | Craft Beer School
desc: Why nitrogen gas gives stouts a dense, creamy head and a smooth body, how the special tap works and what the can widget does.
teaser: That slow cascade and thick white head are not magic. They are tiny bubbles of a gas that hates to dissolve.
standfirst: Nitro stouts pour with a cascading cloud and settle under a thick, creamy head. We explain why nitrogen behaves so differently from the CO2 in most beer and what the tap and the widget do to release it.
sections: What makes a nitro beer different

Most beers are carbonated with carbon dioxide. A nitro beer is served with a mix of nitrogen and carbon dioxide, often around 70 to 75% nitrogen. It has noticeably less CO2 than a normal lager, so it feels softer on the tongue.

The result is a beer with a fine, creamy head and a smooth texture. Stouts are the classic example, but brewers also use nitro for porters, red ales and even some pale beers.

Nitrogen is much less soluble in beer than carbon dioxide. Very little of it dissolves, even under pressure. That is the key to everything.

Bubbles in beer tend to merge over time. Gas moves from small bubbles into large ones, so the foam coarsens and collapses. CO2 moves quickly between bubbles because it dissolves easily. Nitrogen moves slowly because it does not.

So nitrogen bubbles stay small. Small bubbles make a dense, tight foam that lasts. Our guide to beer foam science explains the proteins and hop acids that help hold it together.

A nitro beer needs a special tap to release its gas. The stout faucet has a restrictor plate, a small disc with several tiny holes, just before the spout.

Beer is pushed through those holes at high pressure. The sudden drop knocks gas out of solution and creates a huge number of tiny bubbles. That is what you see as the cascade, with bubbles appearing to sink down the outside of the glass as the beer settles.

The bubbles are not really falling. The beer near the glass wall moves downwards while bubbles rise in the centre. The effect looks better in a curved glass.

A can has no stout tap, so brewers found another way. A widget is a small plastic capsule inside the can, filled with gas under pressure during canning.

When you open the can, the pressure inside drops. The widget releases a jet of gas and beer through a tiny hole, which starts the bubble cascade much like the tap does. That is why nitro cans often say to pour hard into a glass.

One brewery-floor detail: canned nitro beers are often filled with a drop of liquid nitrogen just before the can is sealed. As it turns to gas, it pressurises the can and helps fill the widget.

Lower CO2 means less carbonic bite, the slight sharp, acidic tingle that carbonated beers have. Roasted malt flavours come across smoother and softer. Some drinkers find hop bitterness less noticeable too.

That suits stouts with plenty of roast and chocolate character. If you want to understand where those flavours come from, our guide to brewing a stout at home walks through the grains.

The creamy texture can make a beer seem richer than it is. A nitro stout is often no stronger than many lagers. Drink it slowly and enjoy the texture.
Why nitro beers taste flat from a bottle

Pour a nitro beer without a widget or a stout tap and it often seems flat and thin. That is because there is so little CO2 and the nitrogen stays mostly in solution. Without a hard jolt to break it out, no creamy head forms.

This is also why you cannot simply add nitrogen to any beer in a home keg and expect the same result. The gas pressure, the beer's CO2 level and the tap all need to match. Brewers set the CO2 level low on purpose before the beer meets the nitrogen mix.

Some brewers now use special nitro taps or ultrasonic devices that send a pulse through a poured beer to trigger the cascade. They work on the same idea: give the dissolved gas a sudden push so tiny bubbles form all at once.
Serving nitro beer at home and in India

Nitro needs the right gas mix and the right tap. A regular CO2 system will not give the same result. Many Indian taprooms that serve nitro keep a separate gas line and faucet for it.

Serve nitro stouts a little warmer than lager, often around 6 to 8 °C, so roast and chocolate notes come through. Very cold serving dulls them. Pour into a clean glass, as any grease kills the head quickly.

Once you understand how gas behaves in beer, you start to see why each part of brewing, from carbonation to serving, is a choice. Our guide to CO2 in the brewery covers how carbonation is managed day to day.
faqs: Why is a nitro stout so creamy?
Nitrogen hardly dissolves in beer, so its bubbles stay tiny and merge slowly. Tiny bubbles make a dense, long lasting head.
What does the widget in a can do?
It holds pressurised gas. When the can opens, it releases a jet that knocks gas out of the beer and starts the cascade.
Is nitro beer stronger than normal beer?
Not usually. The creamy texture can feel rich, but many nitro stouts are no stronger than everyday lagers.
